thread.title: Here's how Bank of America will use tech to enter the Cincinnati market

author: Mark Calvey
title: Here's how Bank of America will use tech to enter the Cincinnati market
text: – Senior Reporter, San Francisco Business Times Aug 10, 2018, 5:51am PDT Bank of America is expanding into new cities with a digital-first strategy, luring local customers with special offers to establish accounts before the first branch even opens. “We’ve changed our approach to new-market expansion. Instead of opening a branch and supporting it with digital, we’re leading with digital,” Michelle Moore , BofA’s (NYSE: BAC) head of digital banking, told the San Francisco Business Times. “With digital, we’re able to reach more customers. We won’t need as many branches, but the branches are still key.” The first new market using the digital-first strategy is Pittsburgh, where the bank pulled prospective customers to its mobile banking services with special offers, local advertising and a dedicated phone line for Pittsburgh customers in early July. The bank’s digital offerings allow customers to open checking accounts and apply for credit cards, mortgages and auto loans. The first branch in the Pennsylvania city opens in late September. Moore said the same strategy will be used when BofA’s first branch opens in other cities: Salt Lake City in early 2019, Columbus and Cincinnati in mid-2019 and later, Cleveland. In recent years, the bank’s new markets for branches have included Denver, Minneapolis and Indianapolis. BofA said branches in Denver, its first market in which it built a branch network from the ground up rather than buying its way into the market, have done well. Nobody is predicting that bank branches will go the way of airline ticketing offices, which were once a common sight in America’s large cities. But bank branches are expected to be smaller and less prevalent as the debut of smartphones more than a decade ago means most people carry their bank in their pocket. BofA and its rivals increasingly see branches as a place for customers to discuss more complex issues like starting a business or creating an investment strategy, while relying on mobile banking and other technology for routine transactions. The digital-first strategy has another benefit for Bank of America: Customers come to the bank expecting to be able to handle most of their business through mobile banking, said Steve Boland , consumer lending executive at BofA, where he’s worked on digital mortgages, mobile car shopping and other initiatives. By contrast, customers used to walking into branches to deposit checks and handle other transactions are being urged to consider using mobile banking. Boland and Moore, both based in Charlotte, were among BofA’s consumer banking executives meeting this week in San Francisco, where Thong Nguyen , president of retail banking and co-head of consumer banking, is based. The executives were among BofA’s leadership team that met with reporters Wednesday to show off some of the latest digital banking enhancements, such as a single-screen showing all of a customer’s various BofA reward program balances in one place. That’s rolling out over the next month or so. The digital banking initiatives are being pursued by teams in San Francisco, Charlotte and elsewhere. Some of the bank’s recent hires suggest that pursuing innovation at some of the nation’s biggest financial institutions might now be considered cool. BofA recently hired Tommy Elliott from Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) as digital payments executive, based in Sunnyvale and San Francisco; Rachel Kobetz came over from Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) as head of design, based in San Francisco; and Nikki Katz joined from the Walt Disney Co. (NYSE: DIS) to be BofA’s digital strategy and transformation executive, based in Los Angeles. Brent Reston , BofA’s head of digital sales, is also based in San Francisco. All four executives report directly to Moore. BofA’s digital-first strategy in new markets is a departure from the bank’s strategy of opening branches in a new market then supporting the physical locations with mobile banking services. BofA’s long-standing approach to expanding into new markets was simply buying a major bank in the region, which eventually allowed the bank to stitch together the nation’s first bank with branches coast to coast when San Francisco’s BankAmerica was acquired by Charlotte-based NationsBank in 1998. But federal regulations no longer allow the nation’s biggest banks to make such sizable acquisitions. That has Bank of America slowly filling in the holes in its branch network. Bank of America hosts some 50 branches within 11 miles of downtown Portland. – Senior Reporter, San Francisco Business Times Aug 10, 2018, 5:51am PDT Related Content
